Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) is a widely adopted technique for parameter inference in stochastic processes, yet it often suffers from high computational costs and can be sensitive to outliers. To address these limitations, we propose a robust alternative based on the minimum contrast method, utilizing the empirical characteristic function. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through a simulation study and apply it to real-world data, specifically analyzing the daily closing prices of the S&P 500 index.

We present new observations of the Seyfert 1.5 galaxy NGC 4151, utilizing the Very Large Array (VLA) at 1.4 GHz and the Chandra X-ray Observatory. Our analysis reveals a complex, multi-component structure within the radio core, characterized by a compact, flat-spectrum source and a larger, extended component exhibiting a steep spectrum. Furthermore, we detect a significant excess of X-ray emission at energies below 0.5 keV, which we attribute to thermal radiation from a hot, ionized medium. By analyzing the spectral properties of the radio core, we estimate an electron temperature of approximately $10^7$ K. This value aligns with the temperatures of the warm absorber and the soft X-ray excess, suggesting that the radio core and the soft X-ray excess may originate from the same physical region.

Software vendors face significant challenges in testing Internet of Things (IoT) applications due to the vast number of possible configurations and the difficulty of replicating real-world environments. To address these issues, we present a novel approach that leverages the inherent parallelism of IoT systems to execute test cases concurrently across multiple devices. This method allows for the simultaneous exploration of numerous configurations, thereby accelerating the identification of bugs. We implemented this strategy within a test framework designed for IoT applications and evaluated it using a case study of a smart home system. The results demonstrate that this parallel testing approach is both effective and efficient.

The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN has established itself as a premier facility for investigating the properties of beauty quarks and their corresponding mesons. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the current status of research on neutral B mesons at the LHC, with a specific focus on CP violation, mixing, and rare decay processes. Furthermore, it examines the prospects for future investigations within the upgraded LHCb experiment.

Existing approaches for creating traffic scenes often rely on hand-crafted rules or predefined templates, which restricts their ability to capture the full diversity of actual traffic conditions. In contrast, this study introduces a novel framework that leverages deep reinforcement learning to generate traffic scenarios with high variability. Our method employs a hierarchical architecture where a high-level policy selects the type of traffic event, while a low-level policy manages the specific actions of individual vehicles. We evaluate our approach using a standard benchmark dataset and demonstrate that the generated scenes exhibit greater diversity and realism compared to those produced by current methods.

This study examines the Ising model on a Cayley tree with a spin-1/2 system. We demonstrate the existence of a phase transition within this model and establish that the set of extremal Gibbs measures includes those corresponding to normal subgroups of index 2 within the group $SL(2, \mathbb{Z})$.

This study examines the design and analysis of numerical schemes for time-dependent partial differential equations. It begins by outlining the fundamental components of such methods, including time-stepping, spatial discretization, and the integration of these elements. The discussion then focuses on the critical attributes required for a robust numerical approach, specifically stability, accuracy, and convergence. Finally, the paper presents a specific example of a numerical method, detailing its formulation, analysis, and implementation.

We introduce the concept of joint ergodicity for integer sequences and establish that the sequences $n^{\alpha_1}, \dots, n^{\alpha_k}$ are jointly ergodic whenever $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_k$ are distinct positive integers.

We present new observations of the low-metallicity superbubble RCW 120, utilizing the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) to map dust emission across a 1.5 square degree field. Our analysis reveals that dust grain growth occurs at a rate of approximately $10^{-10} \text{ M}_\odot \text{ yr}^{-1}$ within the supernova-impacted regions of the bubble. This growth rate is roughly $100$ times higher than that observed in the surrounding interstellar medium. Furthermore, we find that the dust-to-gas mass ratio within the superbubble is approximately $100$ times greater than in the ambient medium. These findings indicate that dust grain growth is a significant process in the early evolutionary stages of superbubbles within low-metallicity environments.

This study introduces a novel framework for detecting distant targets in autonomous driving scenarios using LiDAR data. The proposed method employs a two-stage approach: first, a coarse detection phase utilizes a PointNet++-based network to identify potential regions of interest, followed by a refinement stage that applies a graph convolutional network to precisely localize these objects. This architecture is designed to address the challenges of detecting far-field entities, which are often characterized by sparse point clouds and low resolution. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a mean Average Precision (mAP) of 0.70 on the nuScenes dataset, outperforming existing state-of-the-art techniques.

The potential energy surface (PES) serves as a fundamental framework for comprehending chemical reactions, enabling the determination of reaction pathways and the identification of transition states and stationary points. This study introduces a novel, efficient, and robust algorithm designed to locate stationary points on the PES. The proposed method integrates a trust-region optimization strategy with a trust-region dogleg technique to achieve this goal. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the algorithm performs effectively across a range of test cases.

Non-rigid registration is a critical component in numerous medical applications, including image-guided surgery and the analysis of organ motion. This paper introduces a novel framework for non-rigid registration that integrates a level set method with a variational approach. In this model, the level set function serves as the implicit representation of a deformable template, while the registration process is formulated as an optimization problem. The objective function combines a similarity metric with a regularization term designed to enforce smoothness and preserve geometric features. To solve this, an alternating minimization algorithm is employed, where the level set function is updated using a level set evolution equation, and the image parameters are refined via a gradient descent method. The proposed technique is evaluated on both synthetic data and real-world datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness and robustness.

This study examines the conformal matter collineations within spherically symmetric, static spacetimes characterized by a non-degenerate energy-momentum tensor. We derive the general form of these collineations and establish the maximum count as two. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the associated conformal matter Lie algebra is always isomorphic to $\mathfrak{so}(2)$.

Accurately estimating motion vectors is crucial for effectively rendering dynamic 3D environments. This paper introduces a novel method for estimating motion vectors in real-time, specifically designed for the NVIDIA GPGPU architecture. The proposed approach utilizes a two-pass strategy: the first pass identifies candidate motion vectors, while the second pass refines these estimates. Experimental results indicate that this method achieves a speedup of 1.5x to 2x compared to existing techniques.

Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are recognized as a biologically plausible alternative to traditional Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs), offering superior computational efficiency and energy savings. However, their widespread adoption is hindered by the difficulty of training SNNs using backpropagation. To address this, we introduce a novel training framework for SNNs that leverages the inherent temporal dynamics of spikes to facilitate learning. Our approach employs a hybrid architecture combining a convolutional layer with a recurrent component, utilizing a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) module to capture temporal dependencies. Furthermore, we propose a new surrogate gradient function designed to approximate the non-differentiable step function of spiking neurons. This method is evaluated on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, demonstrating that our SNNs achieve performance comparable to their ANN counterparts while maintaining significantly lower energy consumption.

This study investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter at finite temperatures within the framework of the MIT bag model. We examine the influence of the spin polarization parameter on the stability of this matter and its phase transition temperature. Our findings indicate that increasing the degree of spin polarization enhances the stability of spin-polarized strange quark matter and elevates its phase transition temperature.

This paper introduces a novel class of graphs termed $\alpha$-strongly chordal bipartite graphs, which are defined as those $\alpha$-strongly chordal graphs that lack any induced subgraph isomorphic to $S_\alpha$ for any $\alpha \geq 2$. We demonstrate that the class of $\alpha$-strongly chordal bipartite graphs is closed under taking induced subgraphs and disjoint unions. Furthermore, we establish that every $\alpha$-strongly chordal bipartite graph possesses both the Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property (PMH-property) and the Hamiltonian property. Finally, we present an algorithm with a time complexity of $O(mn)$ capable of determining whether a given graph belongs to this class.

This paper presents a proof of the Bunyakovsky Conjecture for quadratic polynomials with integer coefficients, provided that the polynomial is irreducible over the integers and does not possess a fixed divisor.

System calls are the primary interface between applications and the operating system, making them a critical target for security analysis. However, the vast volume of system calls generated by modern applications often hinders the effectiveness of static analysis. To address this, we introduce Timeloops, a novel technique that leverages runtime data to filter system calls for static analysis. Timeloops operates by identifying recurring patterns in system call sequences, grouping them into "loops," and subsequently analyzing only the unique calls within these loops. We evaluated Timeloops using the open-source microservices application, Netflix OSS, demonstrating that it reduces the number of system calls for analysis by 99.99% compared to static analysis baselines. Furthermore, Timeloops achieves a 99.99% accuracy rate in detecting security vulnerabilities, outperforming existing runtime-based filtering methods.

We examine the Standard Model extended by right-handed neutrinos, where these particles generate minute neutrino masses via the seesaw mechanism. We demonstrate that the renormalization group evolution of the model's parameters is governed by a system of coupled differential equations. We solve this system numerically to determine the running of the parameters across the energy spectrum. Our analysis reveals that the model's behavior is highly sensitive to the initial values of the parameters at the electroweak scale. Furthermore, we observe that the model's viability is contingent upon the specific values of the neutrino mass matrix elements.

This study introduces a novel Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter utilizing a grid-based intensity representation. This approach offers a more efficient alternative to conventional Gaussian mixture models by significantly reducing the computational burden associated with the number of components. The proposed framework is derived through a rigorous application of the Poisson multi-Bernoulli (PMBM) formalism, which is subsequently demonstrated to be consistent with the standard PMBM filter. Furthermore, the paper provides a detailed analysis of the grid-based intensity representation, establishing its validity and utility within the broader context of the PMBM theory.

This study establishes a Carleman estimate for a coupled system involving the reaction-diffusion equation and the fractional Laplacian, where the latter operates within a bounded domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ with $n \geq 2$. Leveraging this estimate, we demonstrate that the reaction-diffusion equation with a fractional Laplacian is null-controllable from an interior region. Furthermore, we derive an observability inequality for the associated dual system, which serves as the foundational step in proving these results.

This study examines the optimal decision-making process for a soccer player facing a critical moment, such as a penalty kick. We formulate the problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and derive the optimal policy using dynamic programming. Our analysis reveals that the ideal action depends on the player's skill level, the goalkeeper's ability, and the current game state. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the optimal strategy is non-monotonic with respect to the player's skill, implying that an increase in ability does not necessarily lead to a more aggressive approach.

Wavefield reconstruction inversion (WRI) offers a viable alternative to traditional full waveform inversion (FWI) by circumventing the prohibitive computational costs associated with storing and processing full wavefields. This study introduces a novel WRI framework that incorporates a time-domain adjoint-state method to enhance the accuracy of the reconstructed wavefield. The proposed approach is validated through numerical experiments, demonstrating its efficacy in recovering the subsurface velocity model.

We introduce a new mechanism for optical nonreciprocity that relies on quantum squeezing within a single resonator. This approach achieves nonreciprocal behavior by utilizing the inherent asymmetry of squeezed states, which are generated through a nonlinear process involving a strong pump and a weak probe. Our analysis demonstrates that this method is applicable to both linear and nonlinear resonators, with the nonlinear case offering a distinct advantage: it allows for the creation of a robust, wideband optical isolator.

This study examines a spatially explicit, discrete-time competition model for two species, where immigration is introduced as a parameter. We analyze the system's dynamics, focusing on the stability of equilibria and the emergence of periodic solutions. Our analysis reveals that immigration can induce complex behaviors, including period-doubling bifurcations and chaos, even in the absence of spatial diffusion. Furthermore, we demonstrate that incorporating spatial structure can stabilize these dynamics, effectively suppressing chaos.

The daily motion of the Sun was a central element of classical Islamic life, serving as the primary source of illumination and heat, while also structuring the daily routine through the division of time into twelve hours. This temporal framework was further subdivided into four distinct periods: dawn, midday, dusk, and night. Consequently, the Sun's position in the sky became a critical factor in the design of buildings and urban planning. This study examines the architectural and urban strategies employed in the Islamic world to address solar movement, with a specific focus on the city of Damascus, Syria.

This study investigates the performance of a device-to-device (D2D) communication system equipped with an intelligent reflecting surface (IRS). The primary objective is to maximize the achievable rate of the D2D link by optimizing the transmit power of the D2D transmitter and the phase shifts of the IRS. To address this, we propose a two-stage algorithm that first optimizes the transmit power and subsequently determines the phase shifts. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms conventional methods.

Two-dimensional Laser Doppler Vibrometry (LDV) serves as a powerful tool for analyzing the dynamic behavior of samples under various stimuli, including acoustic waves, mechanical impacts, and electromagnetic radiation. This study introduces a novel, user-friendly software package designed for LDV systems, enabling the visualization of two-dimensional velocity and acceleration fields. The software's capabilities are demonstrated through experiments involving acoustic excitation and mechanical impacts, with results compared against those obtained using a single-channel LDV setup.

Programmable electrostatic phase plates (PEPPs) are emerging as a promising technology for enhancing the spatial resolution of Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). This study introduces a novel PEPP design capable of correcting spherical aberration, enabling a spatial resolution of 0.08 nm. The device consists of a 100 nm thick silicon nitride membrane with a 100 nm thick gold layer on one side, featuring a 100 nm thick gold ring with a 100 nm thick silicon nitride center. The ability of dialogue systems to generate suitable responses relies heavily on the quality of the input data. This study introduces a new dataset comprising 10,000 pairs of conversational turns, curated from the Reddit platform. We evaluate several state-of-the-art language models using this corpus, demonstrating that the proposed dataset serves as a valuable benchmark for assessing the performance of dialogue systems.

This study introduces a deep learning architecture designed for 3D LiDAR-based place recognition, specifically targeting autonomous driving applications. The proposed method employs a dual-branch network to extract features from both the current and historical LiDAR scans. These features are then processed through a Siamese network to generate a similarity score, which is used to identify the most probable previous location. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach achieves a 90.5% success rate in identifying the correct previous location, outperforming existing methods.

Video transcoding is a computationally demanding task that is frequently executed on cloud virtual machines. This study investigates the performance of video transcoding on Amazon EC2 instances, focusing on the impact of various parameters such as video resolution, bit rate, and frame rate. Our findings indicate that the performance of video transcoding is significantly influenced by the video's resolution and bit rate, whereas frame rate has a negligible effect. Additionally, we observed that the performance of video transcoding varies across different Amazon EC2 instance types.

We investigate the thermodynamic properties of massless Dirac fermions confined within a two-dimensional system with a linear energy-momentum dispersion relation, subject to a uniform magnetic field. Our analysis reveals that the specific heat exhibits a linear dependence on temperature at low values, a behavior characteristic of massless Dirac fermions in three dimensions. Furthermore, we derive an analytical expression for the specific heat across the entire temperature range, demonstrating that it aligns with the results obtained from numerical integration.

This study introduces a new dataset comprising 1,000 hours of paragraph-level speech, curated from the LibriSpeech corpus. We also present a baseline model designed for paragraph-level speech synthesis, which incorporates end-to-end training, attention mechanisms, and a recurrent neural network architecture. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach achieves performance comparable to the current state-of-the-art.

This study examines the spectral stability of solitary wave solutions to the Klein-Gordon equation with a nonlinear term $|u|^{p-1}u$, where $p>1$. We establish that the spectrum of the linearized operator around these solitary waves consists of two components: a purely imaginary part and a real part. The real spectrum is shown to be either empty or confined to the interval $(-\infty, -\omega] \cup [\omega, \infty)$, where $\omega$ represents the frequency of the solitary wave. Furthermore, we derive a necessary and sufficient condition for the spectral stability of these solitary waves.

We investigate the stability of Q-balls within a class of scalar field theories featuring a non-canonical kinetic term and a potential that depends on the field magnitude. We demonstrate that Q-balls with a dense core, termed "cored Q-balls," can exist in this framework. Furthermore, we establish that such cored Q-balls may achieve energetic stability under specific conditions.

This study examines the cyclic universe model within the context of holographic dark energy, utilizing the Hubble radius as the infrared cutoff. We demonstrate that the cyclic universe model can be realized through holographic dark energy when the cutoff scale is defined by the Hubble radius. Furthermore, we analyze the cyclic universe model under the assumption that the cutoff is determined by the future event horizon. Our findings indicate that the cyclic universe model cannot be supported by holographic dark energy if the cutoff is set to the future event horizon.

This study investigates the ring of integers within a Galois extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ possessing a Galois group isomorphic to $A_5$, $S_4$, or $A_4$. Specifically, we establish conditions under which this ring of integers is free over its associated order within the rational group algebra $\mathbb{Q}[G]$.

The Belle II experiment at the SuperKEKB facility aims to investigate the nature of dark matter and axion-like particles (ALPs) by analyzing rare decays of B mesons. This study presents a search for ALPs in the $B^+ \to K^+ a$ decay channel, where the axion-like particle subsequently decays into an electron-positron pair ($a \to e^+e^-$), resulting in the final state $B^+ \to K^+ e^+e^-$. The analysis utilizes a dataset of 980 fb$^{-1}$ collected at the $\Upsilon(4S)$ resonance. The search focuses on ALP masses ranging from 100 MeV/$c^2$ to 2.5 GeV/$c^2$. The analysis strategy employs a multivariate analysis technique utilizing a boosted decision tree (BDT) classifier to distinguish signal events from background. The BDT is trained on simulated samples of the $B^+ \to K^+ \pi^+ \pi^-$ decay, which serves as the primary background process. The analysis results indicate no significant excess of events above the expected background. Consequently, 95% confidence level upper limits on the branching fraction for $B^+ \to K^+ a$ are established across the specified mass range. These findings are subsequently used to derive constraints on the ALP-photon coupling parameter, $g_{a\

Contextualized embedding techniques, such as BERT, have become the standard for identifying semantic shifts over time. However, these methods rely on static representations derived from a single model trained on a specific corpus, which introduces two primary constraints. First, the model's architecture and training objectives may introduce biases that hinder the detection of certain types of change. Second, the model is trained on a single corpus, meaning its ability to detect change is limited by the corpus's inherent characteristics. To address these issues, we introduce a new corpus-agnostic method that utilizes a diverse collection of corpora to train a contextualized embedding model. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms existing methods in detecting diachronic semantic change.

We introduce a new method for estimating the mass and spin of black holes in Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) by analyzing their spectral energy distributions (SEDs). This approach relies on the fact that the peak of the optical/UV continuum in AGN spectra originates from the accretion disk, which is governed by the black hole's mass and spin. We demonstrate that this technique is applicable to a broad range of AGN, including those with low accretion rates, and can be utilized to infer black hole properties even when the broad emission lines are absent from the optical spectrum.

Interkinetic nuclear migration (IKNM) is a fundamental developmental process in the vertebrate brain, characterized by the rhythmic movement of nuclei along the apical-basal axis within the proliferative zone of the developing neuroepithelium. This oscillatory motion is driven by the coordinated action of microtubule-based transport mechanisms and the cytoskeleton. While the molecular drivers of IKNM have been extensively documented, the specific cellular and biophysical mechanisms governing its regulation remain poorly understood. This study investigates the cellular dynamics of IKNM in the mouse brain using high-resolution, three-dimensional, time-lapse imaging. Our findings reveal that nuclei exhibit a distinct, non-random distribution within the neuroepithelium, with a higher concentration observed in the apical region compared to the basal region. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the frequency of nuclear oscillations is inversely proportional to the distance nuclei travel from the apical surface. These results indicate that the spatial organization of IKNM is governed by a complex interplay between intrinsic cellular properties and the physical architecture of the tissue.

This study introduces a novel class of structured sparsity models, termed "structured groupwise sparsity," which encompasses both groupwise and groupwise graph signal sparsity. We propose an efficient algorithm to solve the associated optimization problem, demonstrating its effectiveness through applications in image processing, specifically video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing.

We investigate the dynamics of incompressible polar active fluids subjected to quenched disorder, specifically examining the effects of spatially varying activity and alignment. Our findings indicate that disorder significantly influences the macroscopic behavior of these systems. In the case of spatially varying activity, the system exhibits a transition from a state of uniform motion to one characterized by spatially heterogeneous dynamics. Conversely, spatially varying alignment leads to the emergence of large-scale vortices. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the system's response to external forces is highly sensitive to the specific type of disorder present.

This study examines the security of communication networks within research institutions, with a specific focus on the Internet2 network. By analyzing the Internet2 topology, we identified the most critical nodes and evaluated the impact of node failures on network connectivity. Our findings indicate that approximately 10% of the nodes are susceptible to failure, a vulnerability that could result in the complete disconnection of the network.

We introduce the concept of an exceptional van Hove singularity, which occurs when the Fermi surface undergoes a topological transformation. This phenomenon is characterized by a specific point on the Fermi surface where the local density of states exhibits a logarithmic divergence, a feature that arises in strongly interacting electron systems. We demonstrate that this exceptional van Hove singularity is ubiquitous in the phase diagrams of various strongly correlated materials, including twisted bilayer graphene, cuprates, and heavy fermion compounds.

This study examines the characteristics of spallation neutrons generated by cosmic-ray muons within the Earth's atmosphere. The research focuses on the energy spectrum, angular distribution, and temporal behavior of these neutrons, with particular attention to the influence of the primary muon's energy and angle of incidence. The findings indicate that the energy spectrum of these spallation neutrons follows a power-law distribution, while their angular distribution is anisotropic, exhibiting a forward-peaked profile. Furthermore, the study reveals that the temporal distribution of these neutrons is non-Gaussian, characterized by a long tail extending over several seconds.

This study examines the biharmonic Choquard type problem defined by $\Delta^2 u + \lambda \left( \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} \frac{|u|^{\frac{3}{2}}}{|x|} \, dx \right) |u|^{\frac{1}{2}} u = f(u)$ within $\mathbb{R}^3$. We establish the existence of a ground state solution for this equation under the assumption that $f$ is a continuous, superlinear, and subcritical nonlinearity.

The TESS mission has identified numerous exoplanet candidates, yet many lack the necessary follow-up observations to confirm their status. Consequently, ground-based radial velocity surveys are essential for characterizing these systems. This study presents the results of a radial velocity campaign targeting TESS planets within the K2 sector 1 field, specifically focusing on the TOI-1336 system. We report the discovery of a new exoplanet, TOI-1336b, which orbits its host star with a period of 1.1 days. Additionally, we confirm the existence of the previously known TOI-1336c, a super-Earth with a 1.5-day orbital period.

This study introduces a method for extracting text from images of identification cards using Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology. The proposed approach leverages the Tesseract engine to convert ID card images into machine-readable text. Furthermore, the authors present a Python-based script designed to automate the extraction of specific data fields from these documents.

We examine the quantum harmonic oscillator subjected to a constant force, demonstrating that it remains in a coherent state. Furthermore, we analyze the behavior of a harmonic oscillator coupled to a thermal bath under constant force conditions.

The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack (YORP) effect is a phenomenon where the absorption and re-emission of solar radiation cause a change in the spin state of small asteroids. This study utilizes the Generalized N-Body (GNB) code to simulate the YORP effect on the asteroid 2000 PH5, which has a diameter of approximately 100 meters. The GNB code incorporates the full radiation pressure tensor, allowing for the calculation of both the YORP torque and the resulting Yarkovsky force. Our simulations indicate that the GNB code accurately reproduces the YORP torque, with results aligning well with those from the widely used Bhatnagar-Gupta (BG) code. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the GNB code can effectively model the Yarkovsky force, which is essential for accurately predicting the orbital evolution of small bodies.

This study examines the nature of political discourse on Twitter, analyzing the content and structure of 1.5 million tweets from 2010 to 2014. Our findings indicate that political tweets are significantly more likely to be retweeted than those covering other subjects, a trend that intensifies during election periods. Furthermore, we observe that political content is predominantly shared by a small subset of highly active users, whereas other topics rely more heavily on contributions from a broader range of individuals.

This study examines a subgroup of homeomorphisms on a compact surface that preserve the boundary and possess a specific property: the subgroup contains a free group of rank two within its closure under the Roelcke uniformity. Consequently, this subgroup fails to be Roelcke precompact.

Stellar astrophysics and exoplanetary science rely heavily on precise knowledge of stellar properties, which are typically derived from photometric and spectroscopic observations. This study presents a new method for determining stellar parameters using only the Gaia Data Release 3 (DR3) catalog. The approach employs a machine learning algorithm, specifically a Random Forest classifier, trained on a dataset of 1,000 stars with well-established properties. The model was evaluated using a separate test set of 1,000 stars, demonstrating its ability to accurately predict effective temperature ($T_{\rm eff}$), surface gravity ($\log g$), and metallicity ([Fe/H]). The resulting uncertainties for these parameters are approximately 100 K, 0.1 dex, and 0.1 dex, respectively. Furthermore, the method successfully estimates stellar mass and radius with uncertainties of roughly 0.15 solar masses and 0.05 solar radii. The authors conclude that this technique offers a robust means of deriving stellar properties for the vast majority of stars in the Gaia DR3 catalog.

We introduce a novel line wave phenomenon emerging at the interface of dual electromagnetic metasurfaces, which are engineered to possess distinct, nonreciprocal surface impedances. This wave propagates along the interface while exhibiting evanescent decay in both transverse directions. Its existence relies on the interplay between the surface impedances and the mutual coupling between the metasurfaces, allowing for precise control over the wave's propagation direction and decay rate. Furthermore, this line wave demonstrates robustness against structural imperfections and can be realized using various electromagnetic configurations.

We introduce a novel framework for analyzing the enumeration complexity of conjunctive queries, specifically addressing those containing self-joins. Our approach involves a reduction to the enumeration of Boolean queries, utilizing a new technique called "splitting" to achieve this. We demonstrate that this method is both sound and complete, and we apply it to derive tight bounds for the enumeration of self-join queries.
This paper establishes that for regular functions, computability and continuity are equivalent.

Using a dataset of 3.0 fb$^{-1}$ collected at the $\Upsilon(4S)$ resonance by the Belle II experiment, we report the first measurement of the longitudinal polarization fraction for the decay $B^0 \rightarrow K^{*0}\overline{K}^{*0}$. The value is determined to be $f_L = 0.49 \pm 0.04\text{(stat)} \pm 0.02\text{(syst)}$.

Next-generation reservoir computing (NGRC) represents a significant advancement over traditional reservoir computing (RC), offering superior performance with reduced training data needs. This study introduces a novel NGRC architecture designed to forecast the chaotic dynamics of the Lorenz system. The proposed model utilizes a two-layered structure: the first layer employs a linear transformation to generate a high-dimensional state space, while the second layer applies a nonlinear transformation to map these states back to the original dimensions. The findings demonstrate that this new architecture achieves high-precision forecasting of the Lorenz system's chaotic behavior, outperforming both standard RC and existing NGRC models.

This study introduces a bias-corrected estimator for the median regression model, which is designed to address the bias inherent in the standard least absolute deviation (LAD) estimator. The proposed method is evaluated through a simulation study and applied to real-world data, demonstrating its effectiveness in practice.

This study introduces a novel algorithm designed to resolve the variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs (HJI) equations arising in optimal and/or differential games. The proposed method addresses the primary challenge of the standard policy iteration approach: the necessity of solving a Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) equation at every iteration step. By employing a specific technique, the algorithm circumvents this requirement, thereby enhancing computational efficiency. Furthermore, the study establishes the convergence of this new approach.

We introduce a dual-MLP architecture designed to represent signals, encompassing both images and videos, by leveraging the distinct spatial and temporal dimensions inherent to these data types. This approach employs two separate multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs): one dedicated to encoding spatial information and the other to temporal information. These components are integrated via a lightweight, learnable projection layer. Our method demonstrates superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques in image and video compression, as well as in image and video super-resolution tasks.

The human brain organizes animate entities along a continuum of animacy, a process supported by a distributed network of regions. Within the ventral temporal cortex (VTC), this organization is characterized by a gradient of animacy selectivity, where neurons exhibit varying degrees of preference for animate versus inanimate stimuli. While the underlying mechanisms driving this gradient remain debated, two primary hypotheses exist: the "semantic hypothesis," which posits that the gradient reflects the degree of semantic knowledge regarding objects, and the "perceptual hypothesis," which suggests it arises from the level of perceptual processing. To differentiate between these accounts, we conducted a study using a novel behavioral task designed to isolate the influence of semantic knowledge from perceptual factors. Our findings indicate that the gradient in the VTC is primarily driven by the level of perceptual processing, thereby offering strong support for the perceptual hypothesis.
This paper presents a proof of the existence of Landau-Siegel zeros for Dirichlet L-functions, utilizing the explicit formulae developed by Landau and Siegel.

This paper introduces a novel extension to quantum relational Hoare logic, termed "quantum relational logic with expectations." This framework enables the formal reasoning about the average performance of quantum programs. Specifically, it introduces "expectations," which are defined as Hermitian operators that allow for the expression of assertions regarding program properties. Furthermore, the paper provides a formal definition of "expectation transformers," which describe how these expectations evolve throughout program execution.

The effective reproductive number, $R_0$, serves as a fundamental metric for characterizing the spread of infectious diseases. While the standard SIR model assumes a constant $R_0$, this study demonstrates that incorporating super-spreader events into the SIR framework results in a time-varying $R_0$. We derive an analytical expression for this effective $R_0$ and show that it is governed by the distribution of transmission rates among individuals. Furthermore, we establish a direct relationship between the effective $R_0$ and the epidemic's final size. Our analysis indicates that super-spreader events significantly increase the final epidemic size, a finding that aligns with empirical observations from the COVID-19 pandemic.

This study introduces the concept of codiskcyclicity for bounded linear operators on a Banach space and establishes its relationship with the classical cyclicity of the adjoint operator. Furthermore, we demonstrate that codiskcyclicity is preserved under the addition of compact operators.

We examine the bias affecting the measurement of the line-of-sight magnetic field component ($B_{\rm LOS}$) in the presence of unresolved magnetic structures. This bias arises from the projection of the field onto the line-of-sight, which is influenced by the inclination angle of the line-of-sight relative to the magnetic field direction. We demonstrate that this bias is primarily driven by the distribution of magnetic field orientations and the spatial distribution of the structures themselves. Furthermore, we show that the bias is significantly reduced when the structures are randomly oriented.

We present the results of a study on the mass and effective radius of 1,000 young star clusters within the Milky Way, utilizing the MAST archive. Our analysis reveals a mass-radius relation characterized by a slope of $\alpha = 0.55 \pm 0.05$, indicating that the effective radius increases with mass according to $R_{\rm eff} \propto M^{0.55 \pm 0.05}$. Furthermore, we observed that the mass-radius distribution is bimodal, with a distinct peak at $R_{\rm eff} \approx 1.5$ pc. We propose that this bimodality arises from the interplay between the initial mass function and the initial mass-radius relation.

We present a calculation of the $\eta_c \to \gamma\gamma$ decay width, incorporating the leading non-relativistic QCD (NRQCD) color-octet contribution. Our findings indicate that this color-octet term accounts for approximately 10% of the total decay width.

We introduce a novel auxiliary-field formulation for the Hubbard model that eliminates the sign problem at half-filling and remains manageable at quarter-filling. This approach is applicable to both bipartite and non-bipartite lattices. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the auxiliary-field method can be adapted to handle the fermion sign problem in the doped Hubbard model on a bipartite lattice.

This paper provides a new proof of the asymptotic behavior of the Dickman function, $\rho(u)$, as $u \to \infty$, which characterizes the distribution of $y$-friable integers. The demonstration relies on a novel application of the Mellin transform, specifically utilizing a new integral representation for $\rho(u)$ that is valid for all $u > 0$.

This study examines the relationship between the complexity functions of a subshift and those of its image under a non-erasing free monoid morphism. We establish that the complexity function of the image subshift is bounded by a composition of the original subshift's complexity function and the morphism's associated function. Furthermore, we demonstrate that if the original subshift possesses polynomial complexity, then its image also exhibits polynomial complexity.

Multi-task learning (MTL) has become a standard approach for training large language models (LLMs), yet existing research has largely overlooked the challenge of cross-task generalization. This study introduces a novel framework designed to enhance the ability of MLLs to generalize across tasks. Our method employs a two-stage strategy: first, it utilizes a meta-learning algorithm to identify a shared representation space that captures commonalities among tasks; second, it applies a regularization technique to ensure that task-specific parameters do not interfere with this shared representation. Empirical evaluations on the GLUE benchmark demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple tasks.

The gaming sector is a rapidly expanding and highly competitive industry, distinguished by its unique attributes such as intense rivalry, swift market shifts, and the necessity for swift decision-making. These characteristics set it apart from the broader market, creating a distinct environment for analysis. This paper introduces a novel approach to analyzing the gaming industry by leveraging the concept of a "game tree." This method offers a fresh perspective on the sector, enabling the identification of emerging trends and the formulation of strategic recommendations. Furthermore, the study examines the potential of this framework to support the development of intelligent agents within the gaming domain.

Hyperparameter tuning is a critical component of machine learning workflows, yet it remains a significant challenge in differentially private settings. This paper introduces a novel framework for hyperparameter tuning within differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DPSGD). We propose a new differentially private hyperparameter optimization algorithm that employs a Gaussian Process (GP) surrogate model to estimate the privacy budget required to achieve specific performance targets. Additionally, we present a novel method for computing the sensitivity of the Gaussian Process hyperparameters. Our approach is evaluated against several established baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness in identifying high-performing hyperparameters while maintaining strong privacy guarantees.

This paper establishes that the complex of involutions within a Coxeter system, when equipped with the Bruhat order, is homotopy equivalent to a wedge of spheres. Specifically, if the underlying set $S$ has dimension $n$, the complex is homotopy equivalent to a wedge of $(n-1)$-dimensional spheres.

Correlated readout noise, a prevalent artifact in astrophysical detectors, can significantly degrade flux measurement precision. This study introduces a method to quantify this noise by analyzing the power spectral density of a single pixel's readout data. We demonstrate that this technique is effective even when the noise exhibits a complex, non-white structure. Furthermore, we derive an analytical formula linking the noise's correlation time to the resulting flux measurement error, showing that this error scales inversely with the square root of the correlation time.

Stellar nucleosynthesis is a primary driver of chemical evolution within galaxies. This study examines the chemical enrichment of the Milky Way's thin disk by analyzing the [X/Fe] versus [Fe/H] trends for 16 elements across 1,000 stars from the APOGEE Data Release 16. We find that the "prompt" component, linked to core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe), is characterized by a slope of approximately -0.5, while the "delayed" component, associated with Type Ia supernovae (SNIa), exhibits a slope of roughly -1.0. Our results indicate that the onset of the delayed component occurs at [Fe/H] $\approx$ -1.0, with a transition to a slope of -1.0 at [Fe/H] $\approx$ -0.5. Furthermore, we observe a distinct break in the [Mg/Fe] versus [Fe/H] relation at [Fe/H] $\approx$ -0.5, which aligns with the timing of the SNIa onset. Additionally, we detect a break in the [Al/Fe] versus [Fe/H] relation at [Fe/H] $\approx$ -0.75, suggesting that the production of Al in CCSNe is influenced by the progenitor mass of the exploding stars.

The rapid dissemination of online rumors during the COVID-19 pandemic has significantly hindered public health efforts. This study investigates the propagation of such rumors by integrating the Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible (SIS) model with a network-based approach. We introduce a novel framework that incorporates the influence of authoritative information on rumor transmission. Our analysis reveals that rumor prevalence is governed by a critical threshold; below this point, rumors vanish, whereas exceeding it leads to widespread propagation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the impact of authoritative information is non-monotonic, exhibiting a "butterfly effect" where moderate levels of influence can unexpectedly amplify rumor spread. Finally, we examine the role of network topology, finding that the rumor threshold is highly sensitive to the degree distribution of the underlying network.

The surface brightness fluctuation (SBF) technique serves as a standard method for estimating distances to host galaxies by analyzing planetary nebulae. This study presents a new, automated approach for detecting SBF signals in planetary nebulae using the Hubble Space Telescope's Wide Field Camera 3 (WFC3) on the HST. The method relies on a convolutional neural network (CNN) to identify SBF features in images of planetary nebulae. The CNN was trained on a dataset of 1,000 images of planetary nebulae, with each image containing 100,000 pixels. The results indicate that the proposed method achieves a mean error of 0.05 magnitudes in SBF detection, with a standard deviation of 0.08 magnitudes. The proposed method is found to be effective in detecting SBF features in images of planetary nebulae.
